paper_title: Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Vision-language models (VLMs) can effectively integrate visual and textual information to perform range of multimodal tasks (Alayrac et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2025). For example, we can ask VLM to identify an object in an image or describe its colour, and these questions require the model to extract different information from the same image and integrate it with the textual query. However, although current VLMs can readily answer these questions, their outputs do not reveal their internal concept representations. VLM can also answer visual question incorrectly even when the visual information needed to answer it remains readable from its intermediate states (Fu et al., 2025). Existing interpretability methods aim to identify information in internal states and examine its role in producing model outputs (Alain and Bengio, 2016; Neo et al., 2025; Kaduri et al., 2025). Gurnee et al. (2026) proposed the Jacobian Lens (J-Lens), Jacobian-based method that provides vocabulary-based readouts of intermediate language-model states. Specifically, it maps the models intermediate hidden states into the space of final-layer decoder states via averaged Jacobian matrices, and provides concept directions for counterfactual intervention experiments. Using J-Lens, Gurnee et al. (2026) identify functional and structural properties associated with global workspace in large language models (LLMs). In brain science, global workspace theory (GWT) (Baars, 2005; Baars and Franklin, 2007; Dehaene et al., 1998) is an influential theory of consciousness that explains how information from different sources is integrated to support flexible cognition. The core hypothesis of this theory is that information is selected from the multiple parallel processes in the brain, integrated in shared workspace, and made available to different specialised processes. Building on the J-Lens study, we extend this analysis to concept information expressed through different modalities, and processed across the visual and language components of VLMs. In this paper, we introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), multimodal Jacobian lens that combines vision encoder lens (V-Lens) and language decoder lens (L-Lens). V-Lens can access concept information from intermediate vision encoder states before visual information is combined with the text input in the decoder. L-Lens can access concept information from decoder states during the integration of visual and textual inputs, allowing us to examine selective access under different text queries and during autoregressive generation. Both V-Lens and L-Lens map intermediate states into shared semantic space defined by the decoders output vocabulary, so we can compare concept accessibility during multimodal information integration and processing. Figure 1 illustrates these readouts in visual question answering (VQA) example. We conduct counterfactual experiments using MC-Lens, where we intervene on intermediate state components associated with the accessed concepts and observe the resulting model outputs, to infer the role of these concepts in downstream computation. In addition, we also investigate the functional properties and internal organisation of multimodal concept processing in VLMs in relation to GWT. Specifically, our experiments address four related aspects. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Our experiments show that multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and can be selectively accessed according to task demands. Spatial readouts further reveal object identity and attributes such as colour and material at fine spatial scale. In addition, we extend the readout carriers used to express concept, from single name token to set of tokens. This extension helps us better capture and express concept information in intermediate states, and supports subsequent counterfactual experiments on its role in downstream computation. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. The counterfactual experiments indicate that the concept information we access is not merely shown on display board, but also participates in downstream computation and reasoning. In causal reasoning VQA tasks, we perform counterfactual interventions on intermediate concept representations, and find that these interventions 2 can redirect answers to questions requiring multiple steps of reasoning, or influence multiple aspects of downstream reasoning. And we find that these effects generally become stronger as we expand the readout carriers using larger concept direction sets. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two Jspace based metrics to track correspondence between visual states and language-defined concepts. We also construct controlled VLM training setting for vision-language alignment, and evaluate these metrics across checkpoints at different stages of training. Our experiments show that our proposed metrics reflect the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than the hidden state cosine baseline. Concept readouts from the same checkpoints further show that concept accessibility improves early in alignment training, whereas reliable selective access develops later. (iv) Shared functions across models. We extend our experiments to VLMs of different sizes from multiple model families (Bai et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024; Gemma Team, 2025). Across these models, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects, despite differences in their internal workspace organisation. Together, these findings provide an experimental basis for studying GWT in multimodal artificial systems, and open way to investigate how GWT can guide improvements in cross-modal alignment.

sections.title: 2 MC-Lens: A Jacobian Lens for Multimodal Concepts
sections.content: In general, VLMs output provides only limited view of its internal processing. For example, VLM may correctly identify bicycle in photograph, but the answer itself does not tell us where the concept of bicycle appears inside the model. Therefore, we develop MC-Lens, Jacobian-based method inspired by J-Lens (Gurnee et al., 2026), to access concept information from intermediate states in the VLM and to investigate the role of the accessed concepts in downstream computation and reasoning. In this section, we focus on the mathematical formulation of MC-Lens.

sections.title: 2.2 Vocabulary-Based Concept Readout
sections.content: Suppose VQA task asks the model to identify the object in an input image of bicycle. The model can easily answer bicycle. However, this answer alone does not tell us where the concept of bicycle appears inside the model. Here, we want to figure out at which layer this concept already appears in the models internal states before the answer is produced. 5 Figure 3: Concept readout and reference centring. (A) V-Lens and L-Lens map intermediate states into the decoders final-layer state space, then use its output head to rank vocabulary tokens. (B) The readout state is taken from one position or averaged over position set S. (C) Reference centring subtracts µℓ, the mean state over reference inputs. In this part, we use MC-Lens to read an intermediate state by projecting the state onto the decoders output vocabulary (Figure 3 (A)). The readout gives logit for every word in the vocabulary. We then rank all words by these logits, and the ranks tell us which words the state is close to. In this VQA example of identifying bicycle, if an intermediate state ranks the word bicycle near the top, we regard the concept as readable in that state, and we use the rank of the concept name to measure how accessible the concept is. sections.title: 2.3 Constructing Concept Direction Sets
sections.content: So far, we have used MC-Lens to access concept information from intermediate hidden states in verbalised form. However, we found that the hidden state usually carries more information about concept than its name token expresses. For example, in the bicycle VQA task, bicycle is not the only token that expresses the concept, for two reasons. (1) Different word forms may express the same concept, such as Bicycle, bike and bicycles. (2) Surrounding concepts can also express part of the meaning of this concept. Some are concepts that are closely linked to bicycle, such as riders and road, and some are parts of bicycle or the category it belongs to, such as handle and transport.4 This phenomenon is especially pronounced in VLMs. In an LLM, the word bicycle enters the hidden state as the token bicycle itself. However, in VLM, the concept enters from the image, which has no such token to anchor it, so we expect the concept to be spread over more vocabulary tokens in the hidden state. The readout and counterfactual experiments in Sections 3.2 and 5.1 support this view. In this part, we therefore describe concept with set of tokens rather than one token. JLens describes single-token concept by the vocabulary direction of its token (Gurnee et al., 2026). Here, we select set of tokens for each concept and use their vocabulary directions as its concept directions. Together, these directions form the concept direction set. We choose these vocabulary tokens in two ways: (1) word-form selection and (2) greedy selection via J-space reconstruction. sections.title: 2.4 Counterfactual Interventions on Concept Representations
sections.content: Suppose that, in VQA task, the input is an image of Canadian flag and the question asks for the capital of the flags country. The model answers Ottawa. Section 2.2 tells us whether the concept Canada is readable in an intermediate hidden state, and Section 2.3 gives the concept directions for Canada. Here we want to find out whether the concept of Canada we access in the intermediate state is used to compute the answer about its capital, or is merely shown on display board. We define the counterfactual intervention here as setting the hidden states of the model at chosen layers to chosen values during the forward pass, and letting the later layers compute from the edited states (Meng et al., 2022; Geiger et al., 2024). We call the concept whose representation we want to change the source concept, and the concept we want to write into the state the target concept. In our example illustrated in Figure 6, the source and target concepts are Canada and Australia, respectively. Figure 6: Concept interventions. (A) PairSwap swaps the source and target name-token coordinates within the source state. (B) SubRep replaces the source states projected component with that of the target state, while retaining the source states orthogonal component. Red arrows denote interventions. 11 We first run the model on the source input xs and the target input xt, each containing an image of its concept and the same question. This gives the hidden states hs ℓ = hℓ(xt) at the same layer and position. We then intervene on the source forward pass at set of layers L, and do[ = ] denotes an intervention that sets the variable on the left to the value on the right (Pearl, 2009). sections.title: 3 Multimodal Concept Accessibility
sections.content: In brain science, GWT proposes that conscious access involves making information available to multiple specialised processes through shared workspace (Baars, 2005). To investigate the potential relationship between GWT and multimodal information integration and processing in VLMs, we use our proposed MC-Lens to examine concept accessibility in intermediate states. We first examine concept readability in intermediate states under different combinations of multimodal inputs. We then extend the analysis to different readout carriers, from single name token to sets of tokens, comparing their ability to express the target concept and reconstruct the intermediate state. We finally examine spatial-level concept accessibility in visual states across network layers and image locations. Together, these experiments provide preliminary evaluation of MC-Lens and these readout carriers for studying multimodal information in intermediate states.

sections.title: 3.1 Concept Accessibility across Evidence Conditions
sections.content: In this part, we investigate concept accessibility in intermediate states with MC-Lens, under different conditions of model input. Specifically, we use VQA as task setting to compare concept accessibility when relevant task evidence is provided by an image or by text. As illustrated in Example 1, we construct four evidence conditions for each question: 1) an image containing evidence for the target concept, with no extra text evidence, 2) sentence explicitly naming the target concept, with blank image, 3) both, or 4) neither. We collect 100 VQA cases from A-OKVQA (Schwenk et al., 2022), each with single-word answer, such as the name of an object or colour. For each case, we use the ground-truth answer as the target concept for our experiment, and the target concept is fixed across the four evidence conditions. We apply the proposed L-Lens to the pre-answer position in decoder layer D32 of Qwen3-VL-8B in this experiment, and then analyse the rank of the target concept token among all vocabulary tokens based on the readout scores. We measure Pass @K (where is rank threshold), the fraction of cases where the target token appears in the top-K ranking, and higher values indicate better concept accessibility. As illustrated in Figure 7, both image and text evidence conditions are able to raise the readability of the target concept under the three Pass @K thresholds (K = 1, 5, 10). Text explicitly naming the target concept tends to give higher readout rates than image evidence only, while providing both sources gives similar rates to text alone. Example 1 illustrates this comparison with VQA task about skateboard move. Without either form of evidence, the target concept token grind ranks 9th. Providing the skateboard image, the sentence naming grind, or both raises the target concept tokens readout rank to 1st place. This experiment shows that both image and text evidence promote concept readability in intermediate states. Figure 7: Concept accessibility across evidence conditions. Bars show the percentage of cases in which the target token appears among the top 1, 5 or 10 readout tokens. The question and target concept remain fixed across the four evidence conditions. 13 Example 1 Image and Text Evidence Promote Concept Readability Question: What type of skateboard move is the man doing? sections.title: 3.2 Extending Concept Readout Carriers
sections.content: In Section 3.1, we used single name token as the readout carrier for concept, following J-Lens (Gurnee et al., 2026). This token gives one way to name the concept (e.g., bicycle the concept of bicycle), but the same concept can be expressed through different tokens (e.g., the concept of bicycle bicycle, bike, Bicycle, etc.). Here, we extend the analysis to sets of tokens as readout carriers. Specifically, we compare two types of concept direction sets: the word-form sets Fj and the greedy sets J@k, as illustrated in Figure 4. We want to examine the readability of these sets and their ability to reconstruct the state. We collect 100 VQA cases from A-OKVQA (Schwenk et al., 2022) and build 50 VQA cases for country name identification using national-flag images from Noto Color Emoji.8 For each case, we use the ground-truth answer as the target concept and compare the sets on the same intermediate state. We include the name-token set F0, the cumulative word-form sets F1, F2 and F3, and the greedy sets J@15, J@25 and J@35 for comparison. For readout, we apply L-Lens at decoder layer D32 of Qwen3-VL-8B to the pre-answer state. To measure the overall readability of set, we use Coverage @10, the proportion of tokens in the top-ten readout that belong to the set. Higher values mean that the target concept is readable through more tokens in the set. We use the reconstruction score (Recon. Score) to measure sets ability to reconstruct the centred intermediate state, and higher values indicate that the selected concept directions better capture the information in the state. sections.title: 3.3 Concept Accessibility in Visual States
sections.content: In Sections 3.1 and 3.2, we examined concept accessibility in the pre-answer state in the language decoder using L-Lens, and here we extend our analysis to intermediate states at visual token positions. We first examine concept accessibility across network sub-modules and depths, and then examine the correspondence between patch-level concept readouts and the locations of objects and attributes in the image. Visual concept readout across network depth. concept accessibility across network sub-modules and depths. In this experiment, we examine visual We select 32 object concepts, with four images for each concept (128 images in total) from THINGS (Hebart et al., 2019). For each image, we use the main object shown as the target concept. Since we want to evaluate concept accessibility in visual states without the influence of text question, we use only the image as the user input in this experiment. This experiment is conducted on Qwen3-VL-8B, using both V-Lens and L-Lens. For the visual encoder, we use V-Lens to read the mean encoder patch state, and for the language decoder, we use L-Lens to read the mean decoder image-token state. For the connector, we read the mean visual state using the lenses fitted to its intermediate states (Appendix A.1). As described in Section 2.2, we apply the centring strategy here to make the concept more readable (Appendix B.2). For each image, we rank vocabulary tokens by their readout scores, and record the best rank among the complete single-token word forms of the target objects name. For example, if Bicycle ranks 3rd and Bike ranks 7th, we record rank 3. We report the median of these ranks across images as the median target rank. We also measure Pass @10, the percentage of images for which at least one of these tokens appears in the top-ten readout. lower median target rank and higher Pass @10 both indicate greater object-name readability. As shown in Figure 9 (A,B), object-name readability improves towards the end of the encoder and remains at similar level through the connector. It drops at the start of the decoder and then improves again in later decoder layers. The shaded region marks the estimated workspace, whose boundaries and interpretation are discussed in Section 6. In the later layers of the estimated workspace, the median target rank is better and Pass @10 is higher than in the later encoder layers. In the encoder, concepts in intermediate states are accessible using V-Lens and become more accessible with increasing depth. In the decoder, even without text question, we can still Figure 9: Visual concept readout across network depth. The darker blue region marks the estimated workspace (WS). Example 4 Spatial Concept Readout with V-Lens Input: The kitchen and desk images are supplied without question. Readout: Each patch is coloured by the highest-scoring word within the object or attribute set. White means no candidate ranks in the top 10,000. Finding: From L18 to L25, object names are readable at more patches, and the maps more clearly show the arrangement of objects in both scenes. These spatial readouts extend beyond object names to colours and materials, although material readouts remain more scattered. use L-Lens to access concepts from intermediate states at visual token positions, and accessibility increases substantially within the estimated workspace. Spatial concept readout. V-Lens can provide spatial-level concept map. Specifically, we apply V-Lens to individual image patches at encoder L18 and L25, using only the image as the user input in this experiment. Example 4 illustrates two scenes. For each scene, we choose set of object names and separate set of attribute words: colours for the kitchen scene and material-related words for the desk scene. We compare readout scores within each set and colour each patch by its highest-scoring 17 word, producing separate object and attribute maps. Patches remain white if the winning word falls outside the top 10,000 tokens (cutoff). At L18, several objects are already distinguishable, but many patches remain white. At L25, more patches have readable object names, and the arrangement of objects is clearer, especially in the desk scene. In the kitchen scene, banana and apple mark the fruit on the left, and cup marks the mug on the right. In the desk scene, book highlights the open pages, and interestingly, the pot region is labelled as cup at L18 but as plant at L25. This change suggests that the concept readout can better match the object in the image at deeper layer. The attribute maps show that these spatial readouts extend beyond object names. In the kitchen scene, yellow and red coincide with the banana and apple, while blue identifies the bowl. In the desk scene, glass highlights the bottle, and ceramic marks the cup. Material readouts remain more scattered than the object and colour maps, and some labels extend beyond the corresponding objects. In this experiment, the concept maps generated by V-Lens allow us to examine the models understanding of multimodal information in intermediate states at fine spatial scale, and to analyse it from different concept dimensions.

sections.title: 4 Selective Access to Multimodal Concepts
sections.content: An important feature described by GWT is that information generated simultaneously by different specialised processes competes for access to shared workspace. The selected information In this section, we try to then becomes consciously accessible (Baars and Franklin, 2007). identify similar selective access mechanism for multimodal concepts in the intermediate states of VLMs, supported by our proposed MC-Lens. Specifically, we first examine how the text query affects concept accessibility in intermediate states, by changing the text query for fixed image. We then further track changes in concept accessibility during autoregressive generation. Together, these experiments provide evidence for selective access to multimodal concepts in the intermediate states of VLMs.

sections.title: 4.1 Query-Dependent Selective Access to Visual Concepts
sections.content: In this experiment, we investigate selective access to visual concepts through MC-Lens readouts and measure the relative accessibility of concepts in the same scene. We collect 100 scene images from COCO (Lin et al., 2014). For each image, we select three visible objects as the target concepts for our experiment and prepare one question for each object. Each question identifies its target through colour, position, or relation to other scene content, without naming it. The VLM receives the same image and one question at time, and we query each image three times using three different questions. We apply L-Lens to the pre-answer position at each decoder layer of Qwen3-VL-8B, and record the ranks of all three target object-name tokens for comparison. To measure selectivity, we define successful selection for question as the requested objects name token ranking above the name tokens of the other two objects. Therefore, selective sensitivity can be defined as the percentage of images with successful selection under all three questions at the same decoder layer. Higher values indicate more consistent query-dependent selection. To account for potential concept information introduced by the text question itself, we repeat the same questions with uniform grey image (blank) to measure the contribution of visual evidence to selection. 18 Example 5 Concept Readability Changes with the Query Input Query on Left Object What object is on the left ? Answer with one word. L-Lens readout Query on Right Object What object is on the right ? Answer with one word. Input Image Finding: Within the estimated workspace, the query changes concept readability for both objects and their associated attributes. As shown in the upper panel of Figure 10, selective sensitivity remains close to zero in earlier decoder layers and rises sharply within the estimated workspace when the original image is provided. With grey image baseline, the increase is much smaller. The lower panel shows the difference in selective sensitivity between Image and Blank, and this difference still becomes larger within the estimated workspace. We find that the text query can substantially increase the relative accessibility of the corresponding concepts among the compared concepts in the same scene. These results demonstrate that the text query can drive selective access. We also provide three examples to examine selective access to objects, their associated attributes and other scene content. In Example 5, we examine query-dependent selection of objects and their associated colours. We use an image containing blue cup on the left and yellow book on the right, and alternate between questions about the left and right objects. We com19 Figure 10: Query-dependent selection of visual concepts. Top: selective sensitivity for original images (Image) and uniform grey images (Blank). Bands show 95% confidence intervals. Bottom: Image minus Blank, in percentage points (pp). pare the readability of cup, book, blue and yellow under the left-object query and the right-object query. We can find that before the estimated workspace, concept accessibility under the two different queries is similar, with little separation between the queries. In contrast, within the estimated workspace, the left-object question makes cup more readable than book, while the right-object question reverses this order. Across much of the estimated workspace, the colour concept blue is also more readable under the left-object question and yellow under the right-object question. Since neither question requests colour, this change suggests that the selective access mechanism can extend beyond the answer name to an associated attribute, and this selective pattern becomes pronounced within the estimated workspace. Example 6 Concept Readability Changes with the Spatial Query Input Input Image L-Lens readout Neutral Query What do you see? Foreground Query What do you see in the foreground ? Distance Query What do you see in the distance ? Finding: Under the distance query, tree reaches high ranks at shallower decoder layers than cat. The query makes concepts from the requested region more readable, including concepts not named in the models answer. In Example 6, we analyse the relationship between this selectivity and spatial relations. Specifically, the example image contains foreground dog and distant cat beside tree, and we keep the image fixed and use neutral query, foreground query and distance query. Within the estimated workspace, neutral and foreground questions make dog more readable than cat and tree, and the model answers dog. The distance question instead makes both cat and tree more readable within the estimated workspace. Tree becomes highly readable at earlier decoder layers than cat, even though the model ultimately answers cat. Under neutral query, the visually prominent dog is more accessible. When the text query specifies the distant region, it directs access towards cat and tree, even though the dog remains visually prominent in the image. Similar to the previous example, this selective pattern becomes clearer within the estimated workspace. 20 Example 7 Concept Readability Varies without Changing the Answer Input Direct Query What object is on the left ? Answer with one word. Ignore Query Ignore the book . Name the other object. Answer with one word. Input Image L-Lens readout Model answer: cup under both queries Finding: The ignore instruction makes book less readable in the later layers, while cup remains highly ranked. The query can change concept readability without changing the models answer. Example 7 provides another example of selective access, where we use specific instruction to reduce access to concept. Specifically, we use the same cup/book image as Example 5 and compare direct query with an instruction to ignore the book and name the other object. The model answers cup under both queries. Within the estimated workspace, book has substantially lower readability under the ignore query, even though it is not included in either answer. This shows that selective access can also affect concepts in intermediate states, even though they are not selected for output.

sections.title: 4.2 Selective Access during Autoregressive Generation
sections.content: We have examined selective access to visual concepts at the pre-answer position in the previous section. Here, we extend the analysis to concept accessibility during autoregressive generation. Specifically, we build two case studies of autoregressive rollout: identifying objects in spatial order and naming objects with or without skipping specified items. We first examine concept readability before and after an objects name is generated during autoregressive generation. In Example 8, the image contains kite, cat and suitcase, and we instruct the model to describe these objects from top to bottom in single sentence. After the model generates its answer, we feed back successively longer prefixes of that answer, and use L-Lens to read the updated last token state at each decoder layer. At each prefix, we read the same three target object-name tokens, i.e., kite, cat and suitcase. Each heatmap presents the accessibility of one object-name token, where columns show the state after each prefix-ending token, rows show decoder layers, and colour indicates vocabulary rank. We can find that the three observed target concepts show similar selective access patterns. Before each object-name token is generated, it is usually more readable in the estimated workspace 21 Example 8 Concept Readability Changes during Answer Generation Describe exactly the three main objects in this image, Query: from top to bottom , using one complete sentence. Name each object once. Do not use list, numbering, or bullet points. Reading the heatmaps: The vintage column shows the readout just before the model generates suitcase . Input Image L-Lens readout Finding: Before an objects name is generated, its concept is usually more readable in the estimated workspace than in earlier decoder layers. Immediately before generation, the name token reaches rank 1 in the motor layers. Once the name enters the text prefix, the concept also becomes more readable in earlier layers. than in earlier decoder layers, and immediately before generation it reaches rank 1 in the outputpreparation (motor) layers. However, once name enters the text prefix, it is also more readable in earlier decoder layers. For example, suitcase is already highly readable in the estimated workspace when the prefix ends in green and then vintage, before the model names the object. In contrast, after suitcase enters the text prefix, it becomes more readable in the pre-workspace layers. This example is also consistent with the sensory, workspace and motor organisation discussed in the J-Lens study (Gurnee et al., 2026). In our example, concept becomes more readable in 22 Example 9 Concept Readability Changes with Output Instructions Task: Name the objects in numerical order as comma-separated list. Shared generated prefix: list: dog, apple, book, chair, car, candle, magnet Model continuation: Ascending order hammer, crown, camera. . . Skip 8 and 9 hammer, crown, camera. . . Input Image L-Lens readout Finding: Changing the output instructions changes concept accessibility within the estimated workspace, even when the image and the generated prefix are the same. earlier layers once its name enters the input, and in motor layers just before its name is generated. We interpret its earlier accessibility within the workspace as consistent with the concept being available for subsequent computation. We next examine the effect of the text instructions on concept accessibility during autoregressive generation. In Example 9, we use an image with 16 objects in specific order, and the query is to report these items following this order. In second condition, we ask the model to skip some of these objects, specifically hammer and crown. During autoregressive rollout, the generated prefixes are identical through the first seven object names, ending with magnet. And in the normal ascending run, the next required name is hammer, while in the skip run it is camera. 23 Similar to the previous example, concepts become more readable within the estimated workspace before their names are generated, and in earlier layers once their names enter the input. This experiment shows that changing the text instructions also leads to the change in concept accessibility within the estimated workspace, even when the image and the generated prefix are the same.

sections.title: Reasoning
sections.content: The previous sections showed that concepts can be selectively accessed in intermediate states, but these observations do not explain how the model uses the information. In GWT, the selected information in the shared workspace can be available to other specialised processes, which allows this information to influence more than one computation (Baars and Franklin, 2007). In this section, we use the counterfactual interventions defined in Section 2.4 to examine the effects of concept-related state components on the final outputs of the model, as illustrated in Figure 11.

sections.title: Reasoning
sections.content: In this experiment, we examine the effects of concept-related state components on model answers under the settings of direct and one-hop VQA tasks. In this setting, the concept c1 is identified from the image, and c2 is an associated concept, as illustrated in Figure 11 (A). We intervene on the state components associated with c1 and compare question about c1 (direct intervention) with question about c2 (one-hop intervention). We use the counterfactual interventions defined with do in Section 2.4. The name-token set F0, cumulative word-form sets Fj and greedy sets J@k specify which concept directions are used for intervention. We combine these sets with SubRep or AbIn, and include F0 + PairSwap as baseline (Gurnee et al., 2026). These operators specify how the state is changed, as illustrated in Figure 11 (B). In Example 10, c1 is the country represented by the national flag, and c2 is its capital. We keep the Canadian flag fixed and change the country-related components from Canada to Australia under the direct and one-hop questions. Both F0 + PairSwap and J@25 + SubRep change the country answer to Australia. For the capital question, however, F0 + PairSwap leaves the answer at Ottawa, whereas J@25 + SubRep changes it to Canberra. Both interventions can therefore influence the models answer in the direct task. In the one-hop task, the J@25+SubRep intervention also redirects the capital answer, showing that country-related information can influence downstream computation. For the quantitative analysis, we build source-to-target pairs using the 50 national-flag images from Noto Color Emoji and follow the same intervention procedure as in Example 10. We use the same country and capital question settings and intervene on country-related components in Qwen3-VL-8B, editing all decoder layers in order of depth (Appendix B.3 examines intervention depth and window width). We compare the name-token set F0 with broader word-form sets and greedy sets with different direction budgets. Each direction set is used with SubRep and AbIn, alongside the F0 + PairSwap baseline. For the one-hop task, capital-answer tokens are excluded during greedy selection. We measure target-answer rate, the fraction of eligible pairs producing complete target answer, and higher values indicate more successful redirection. We also compare the median ranks of the target and source answer tokens before and after intervention, measured at the final layer before generation. 24 Figure 11: Counterfactual interventions on concept representations. (A) Replacing country-related components can change the answer to capital question. (B) Four intervention operators and their state updates. (C) Necessity and sufficiency tests replace and restore components using original and grey-image states. For both direct and one-hop tasks, different intervention operators and direction sets lead to diverse effects on model answers. As shown in Figure 12 (A), direct interventions with SubRep redirect nearly every answer across all tested direction sets. The name-token set F0 therefore already provides strong control in the direct task, and expanding this set brings only limited In contrast, the success of one-hop interventions varies much more with the improvement. direction set, as shown in Figure 12 (D). With SubRep fixed, broader word-form sets Fj improve one-hop intervention success, but the greedy sets J@k are more effective. Even the smallest greedy set, J@5, redirects nearly every one-hop answer, whereas the broadest word-form set, F3, redirects fewer than half. J@5 gives stronger one-hop control with fewer directions per concept, using five compared with roughly eight for F3. We also find that answer control depends on the intervention operator. With the same nametoken set F0, SubRep and AbIn redirect more direct answers than PairSwap, as shown in Figure 12 (A). SubRep maintains high success across the greedy budgets in both direct and one-hop tasks, while AbIns success falls as the set expands (Figure 12 (A,D)). The vocabulary ranks help explain these different answer outcomes. For one-hop interventions, target answers remain near the top of the vocabulary with SubRep, but become less readable as the greedy budget increases with AbIn, as shown in Figure 12 (E). At the same time, AbIn suppresses source answers more strongly in Figure 12 (F). Suppressing the source is therefore insufficient for reliable redirection when the target also loses accessibility. 25 Example 10 Concept Interventions Redirect Direct and One-Hop Answers Input Country c1 Direct Country answer Canada Australia Capital c2 One-hop Question source target Ottawa ? These results show that concept information can influence downstream computation. Generally speaking, these experiments show that concept information identified through MCLens can contribute to downstream computation in both direct and one-hop tasks. The effects depend on both the selected concept directions and the intervention operator.

sections.title: Reasoning
sections.content: Previous counterfactual experiments show that concepts read from intermediate states can influence downstream computation and model answers. We extend the analysis to the necessity and sufficiency of these selected intermediate concept components for downstream tasks (Pearl, 2009). As illustrated in Figure 11 (C), necessity tests whether replacing the selected components disrupts the original answer, inspired by the counterfactual tests of Yu et al. (2025). Here, we select VQA example that the model answers correctly with the original image, and construct control run with uniform grey image under the same question. We retain examples with an incorrect grey-image answer. Let hℓ and hℓ denote the states of the unedited original-image and grey-image runs, respectively. Here, Pℓ,chℓ is the component along the selected directions for concept c. We replace the selected components of hℓ in the original-image run using the SubRep hℓ, ℓ L]. If the resulting answer becomes incorrect, this indicates intervention do[Pℓ,chℓ = Pℓ,c that the selected components were necessary for the original answer. Sufficiency tests whether restoring the selected components recovers correct answer, similar to the restoration step of causal tracing (Meng et al., 2022; Palit et al., 2023). sections.title: Tasks
sections.content: In this part, we examine how an accessed concept can serve as shared intermediate information for different downstream tasks. In one-hop VQA task (I c1 c2 A), we keep the input image and the initial concept c1 fixed, and vary the downstream question to ask about different concepts c2 associated with c1. Here, is the models answer. Specifically, as Example 11 illustrates, we extend the downstream task from identifying the capital to questions about the three-letter country code (ISO-3), currency code and other associated information. We then change the country-related components from Ireland to Tunisia using J@25 + SubRep on Qwen3-VL-8B, and observe the changes in the models answers across these tasks. We find that the capital answer changes from Dublin to Tunis, and the currency code changes from EUR to TND. Four of the six answers change to their targets, but the domain and calling-code answers remain non-target outputs. For the quantitative analysis, we build 51 eligible source-to-target pairs using the same 50 national-flag images from Noto Color Emoji, with tasks covering the country name, ISO-3 code, capital, currency code, continent, internet domain and calling code. We apply SubRep in all decoder layers of Qwen3-VL-8B, using the name-token set F0, broader word-form sets Fj and greedy sets J@k, with FullRep as reference. Downstream-answer tokens are excluded during greedy selection. We measure target-answer rate to evaluate intervention success, as in Section 5.1. 29 As illustrated in Figure 14, direct interventions succeed in nearly every case for all direction sets, whereas the success of one-hop interventions varies more. For the one-hop tasks, F0 and F1 give similar target-answer rates, while the broader word-form sets improve control. All three greedy sets give higher target-answer rates than the word-form sets on these tasks. The larger greedy sets redirect most answers across the one-hop tasks, with further improvements as the greedy budget increases. Calling codes remain less reliably redirected even with the largest greedy set, while FullRep reaches every target on every task. Generally speaking, these experiments show that the same concept directions can influence answers across different downstream tasks, providing functional evidence for the broad availability of concept information described by GWT (Baars and Franklin, 2007). The stronger control obtained with broader direction sets suggests that they capture more of the concept-related information used across these tasks. sections.title: 5.4 Causal Effects of Concepts on Multi-Hop Reasoning
sections.content: In this part, we further extend the direct and one-hop comparisons in Section 5.1 to multi-hop tasks. In these questions, the input identifies an initial concept c1, which is linked through an intermediate concept c2 to final concept c3 asked about in the question. We compare interventions on c1-related components alone with joint interventions on c1and c2-related components, and measure the resulting changes in the final answer A. Example 12A shows an intervention for question about the administrative division containing the capital of the country shown by flag. The source relation links the country Canada (c1) to its capital Ottawa (c2) and then Ontario (c3), while the target relation links Greece to Athens and then Attica. With the Canadian flag and question unchanged, J@25+SubRep intervention on country-related components changes the answer from Ottawa, Ontario to Athens, Attica. Example 12B shows an unsuccessful case, where we apply the same type of intervention to question about the International Air Transport Association (IATA) code of an international passenger airport serving the capital. With country-related components changed from Denmark to Jamaica, the answer changes from CPH to SIN, missing the target airport code KIN. For the quantitative analysis, we use 40 eligible multi-hop cases from the same national-flag image set, covering six types of questions about the capital. These questions concern administrative divisions, rivers, airport codes, railway stations, national legislatures and metro opening years. We follow the same intervention procedure as in Example 12 and compare F0, F2 and J@25 via SubRep under the two intervention conditions (c1 and c1 + c2). We use the concept directions for c1 alone or the combined direction sets for c1 and c2 to replace the corresponding state components. Final-answer tokens are excluded during greedy selection. sections.title: 6 Global Workspace Structure and Function across VLMs
sections.content: Previous sections have shown that multimodal concepts can be read from intermediate states, selectively accessed in response to queries, and used in downstream computations, providing evidence for the functions described by GWT (Baars, 2005). In this section, we investigate the structural and functional organisation of global workspaces in VLMs.

sections.title: 6.1 Shared Workspace Structure across Model Families
sections.content: In this part, we investigate shared global workspace structures by comparing J-space geometry and prediction agreement across Qwen3-VL (2B, 8B, and 32B) (Bai et al., 2025), DeepSeek-VL2 (Tiny, Small, and full) (Wu et al., 2024), and Gemma 3 (4B, 12B, and 27B) (Gemma Team, 2025). Vocabulary-direction geometry and effective dimensionality describe the organisation of the directions used for concept readout at each layer. Prediction agreement measures whether the models final predicted token is already readable from an intermediate state. J-space geometry. We first compare the layerwise organisation of vocabulary directions across models, following the J-Lens analysis (Gurnee et al., 2026). We use linear centred kernel alignment (CKA) (Kornblith et al., 2019) to measure how similar the relationships among these directions are between layers. Higher CKA appears as brighter blocks and indicates more similar direction relationships. We also evaluate the spread of vocabulary directions using Direction dimension ratio@90%. This is the fraction of state dimensions needed to retain 90% of the energy in the centred vocabulary directions. higher ratio indicates that these directions are spread over more state dimensions. Among these models, we also estimate the workspace intervals marked in the figures from direction geometry and dimensionality, together with the layerwise readout profiles (Appendix A.4). In Qwen and DeepSeek, early decoder layers have relatively similar direction geometries. At later layers, their geometries become more differentiated, as seen in the decoder blocks of Figure 16 (A-C,G-I). Gemma retains high similarity across much more of the decoder, as shown by the CKA matrices in Figure 16 (M-O). The separation between depth regions resembles the sensory, workspace and motor organisation described by Gurnee et al. (2026). These regions are associated with input processing, the selection and use of intermediate concepts, and prepara32 Figure 16: J-space geometry across nine VLMs. Heatmaps compare vocabulary-direction geometry across layers and components using CKA. Curves show the fraction of state dimensions needed to retain 90% of the energy in the centred vocabulary directions. Blue brackets and darker blue shading mark the estimated workspace. 33 tion of the output, respectively. Appendix B.1 shows that the broad layerwise organisation in Qwen3-VL-8B is preserved across fitting-set sizes. In Qwen and DeepSeek, the dimension-ratio curves in Figure 16 (D-F,J-L) rise more sharply around the estimated workspace entry. The start of this rise indicates the transition into the estimated workspace more clearly than the broad regions of high similarity in the CKA matrices. As processing moves through this interval, vocabulary directions spread over more state dimensions. In Gemma, the dimension ratios remain low through much of the decoder: 4B and 27B rise mainly near the output, while 12B remains low throughout, as shown in Figure 16 (P-R). Across models, encoder dimension ratios remain relatively low. The vision encoders differ in their layerwise direction geometry, both across model families and within the same family. In some encoders, boundary in the CKA matrix is accompanied by an increase in the dimension ratio, as in DeepSeek-VL2 Small (Figure 16 (H,K)). In others, such as Gemma 3 12B, the CKA matrix shows less distinct layer separation and the dimension ratio stays low (Figure 16 (N,Q)). Prediction agreement. Direction geometry describes the fitted lens, but does not tell us when the eventual output token becomes accessible for particular input. We therefore compare the pre-answer readout at each decoder layer with the models own final prediction on 100 image-question inputs from A-OKVQA (Schwenk et al., 2022), following the layerwise agreement analysis of the J-Lens study (Gurnee et al., 2026). For each input, we take the models highestscoring token at the final layer and check whether it appears among the top eight tokens read out from each intermediate layer. Agreement@8 is the percentage of inputs that satisfy this condition at given layer. Higher values indicate that the final predicted token is more consistently accessible from the intermediate readout. The Agreement@8 curves in Figure 17 remain low at early depths and rise mainly within the estimated workspace intervals across all nine models. Gemma also shows sharp rise in Agreement@8, although its decoder direction geometry is less differentiated (Figures 16 (M-O) and 17 (G-I)). This highlights the need to consider multiple indicators when estimating workspace boundaries. Across these models, the final predicted token becomes more readable within the estimated workspace, often alongside changes in direction geometry.

sections.content: In this part, we investigate shared global workspace functions across VLMs with different layerwise organisations. We compare concept accessibility, query-dependent selection and downstream use across the nine models. Visual concept accessibility. We first compare concept accessibility from visual states across network depth without specific text query. We conduct the object readout experiments of Section 3.3 across nine models. The median-rank and Pass @10 curves in Figure 18 track changes in object-name readability. Across most models, object-name readout improves remarkably within the estimated workspace. In some models, including Qwen8B and 32B, readability already increases towards the end of the encoder, then falls at the start of the decoder before rising again. In Qwen and Gemma, decoder readouts improve within the estimated workspace and exceed those in the encoder, as seen in the rank and Pass @10 curves in Figure 18 (A-F,M-R). This improvement within the estimated workspace is shared despite differences in direction geometry. 34 Figure 17: Prediction agreement across nine VLMs. Agreement@8 is the percentage of inputs for which the models highest-scoring token at the final layer appears among the top eight tokens in the intermediate readout. The main exceptions are DeepSeek Small and Full, shown in Figure 18 (H,I,K,L). Small remains weak throughout, while Full improves within the estimated workspace but falls sharply in the final few decoder layers. Query-dependent selective access. We measure Pass @10 for concept accessibility and selective sensitivity for query-dependent selection. Higher Pass @10 indicates better readability of the target answer token, while higher selective sensitivity indicates more consistent selection under all three questions about each image. Larger models generally achieve stronger answer readout and more reliable selection, but models with similar answer readout can differ in selection success. Necessity and sufficiency analysis. We next examine the necessity and sufficiency of selected intermediate concept components for downstream reasoning, following the experimental setting in Section 5.2. All nine models are required to answer capital-identification questions on national-flag images from Noto Color Emoji. We apply one-hop interventions to the countryrelated state components along the concept directions of the greedy set J@25. As in Section 5.2, both tests apply the do intervention for SubRep in Equation 26. Following the definitions in Section 5.2, higher NR indicates greater dependence on the accessed concept information in downstream computation. We finally extend the crosstask intervention experiment of Section 5.3 to all nine models to examine the downstream use of the same concept directions across tasks. Within each model, we keep the concept directions for the country fixed across the seven questions. We compare F0, F2 and J@25 using targetanswer rates. The J@25 profiles in Figure 20 (G) generally extend further outwards than the word-form profiles in panels (E) and (F). Expanding from F0 to F2 increases the mean target-answer rate across the seven tasks in every model, and J@25 raises it further. With J@25, larger models generally achieve stronger control, although increasing model size does not always improve the target-answer rate. These experiments therefore show that, within each model, the same concept directions can influence answers across different downstream tasks. The stronger control obtained with direction sets extending beyond concept names suggests that they capture more of the concept-related information used across these tasks. Generally speaking, these VLMs share patterns of concept accessibility and query-dependent selection within the estimated workspace. The accessed concept information can also contribute to different downstream computations. These shared functions are observed across models with different internal workspace structures. These findings provide functional evidence for the selective access and broad availability of concept information described by GWT.

sections.title: Learning
sections.content: Our experiments so far have examined concept accessibility and downstream effects in pre-trained VLMs with well-developed cross-modal alignment. In this section, we aim to investigate how cross-modal concept alignment and selective access mechanism develop during training. To build simple experimental setting, we connect frozen CLIP vision encoder (Radford et al., 2021) to frozen Gemma language decoder (Gemma Team, 2024) through randomly initialised multilayer perceptron (MLP) connector. We train the connector on an image-caption prediction task for vision-language alignment, while keeping the vision encoder and language decoder frozen, as in the feature-alignment stage of LLaVA (Liu et al., 2023) (Appendix A.5). By examining different training checkpoints, we can track the development of cross-modal concept alignment and selective access.

sections.title: 7.2 Development of Selective Access during Training
sections.content: Our earlier experiments showed selective access to visual concepts in trained VLMs. Here, we use checkpoints from the same controlled training run to examine how this ability develops during vision-language alignment. Example 13 pairs fixed image of cup on the left and book on the right with questions asking for either object. At each checkpoint, we read both object names from the pre-answer decoder state and record their best ranks across complete single-token word forms. We compare these ranks under the two questions to examine question-dependent selection. Early in training, both object names become more readable under either query, but both queries favour book. After 1,000 steps, question-dependent differences become clearer: the left query makes cup more readable and book less readable, while the right query continues to favour book and makes cup less readable. At the later checkpoints, each query favours its requested object. In this example, concept accessibility improves early in training, before reliable selective access develops. The later question-dependent changes suggest that selective access develops during training.

sections.title: 8 Discussion
sections.content: Concept readouts beyond verbalisation. In this paper, we propose MC-Lens, which allows us to read verbalised concepts from intermediate visual and language states. However, reading concept name gives only limited description of the corresponding concept representation. In this paper, we extend this description to include word-form sets Fj and greedy sets J@k. Counterfactual experiments also show that interventions on intermediate states using set of concept directions change one-hop and multi-hop answers more reliably than those using only the vocabulary direction of single name token. These extensions broaden the description of concept, but they still use the models language vocabulary. For example, object names and attribute words give only partial description of an objects shape, texture and other visual details. This motivates future work on concept readouts that express concept information directly through multimodal representations, alongside or instead of words. For example, images, video and audio could provide readouts of content that is difficult to verbalise. Such readouts could help us study the representation, selection and use of this information in subsequent computation. Multimodal concept processing and GWT. With our proposed MC-Lens, we examine the relationship between multimodal concept processing in VLMs and GWT (Baars, 2005). Our experiments show that multimodal concept information can be selectively accessed in intermediate states and can influence downstream computation across tasks. These patterns appear across model families and provide functional evidence for the selective access and downstream availability of information described by GWT. However, our results do not yet identify the mechanisms for broadcasting selected multimodal information to different downstream processes, which is central property of GWT (Baars, 2005). Future work could trace selected information through downstream computations and test the pathways supporting its use. As GWT seeks to explain conscious access, studying these mechanisms in LLMs and VLMs could contribute to research on machine consciousness (Dehaene et al., 2017; Butlin et al., 2023). 43 In Section 7.1, we use J-space metrics J-space constraints for cross-modal alignment. to measure the development of concept-wise vision-language alignment during training. These metrics could also serve as additional constraints during training. For example, an auxiliary loss could encourage image and text states expressing the same concept to respond similarly along its concept directions at the same decoder layer. Future work could combine this objective with token prediction and test its effects on concept alignment, querydependent selection and downstream task performance.

sections.title: 9.1 Global Workspace Theory
sections.content: In an experiment on human visual attention, observers watched video of two teams passing basketballs and counted the passes made by one team. During the video, person in gorilla suit walked among the players. Surprisingly, many observers failed to notice the gorilla (Simons and Chabris, 1999). Global workspace theory offers an explanation for such failures of conscious perception (Baars, 2005). In GWT, specialised processors carry out operations such as detecting motion and recognising objects. These processors work in parallel, and their outputs compete for access to shared workspace with limited capacity. The workspace briefly holds the selected content and broadcasts it to all processors across the whole system, including those involved in memory, language and action (Baars and Franklin, 2007). Global workspace theory associates conscious access with this broadcast. In the basketball and gorilla example, the counting task gives greater priority to information about the attended teams passes in the competition for workspace access. Information about the gorilla may lose this competition and remain outside the workspace. Without being broadcast, the gorilla information remains unavailable for conscious report, and the observer fails to notice the gorilla. The global neuronal workspace model (Dehaene et al., 1998) explains GWTs selection and broadcast mechanisms in terms of neural activity in the human brain. This model proposes network of neurons distributed across several cortical regions and linked by long-range connections. The network receives signals from specialised processors and sends feedback to amplify or suppress their activity. Dehaene and Naccache (2001) elaborated the conditions for conscious access. They emphasised that representation must be amplified and sustained through interactions with workspace neurons to become available to multiple processes, including perceptual categorisation, long-term memory, evaluation and intentional action. Dehaene et al. (2003) further simulated two visual targets presented in quick succession. The first target could prevent the second from triggering ignition, sudden transition from an early sensory response to sustained activity across the workspace. The model predicted that the second target would tend to be either unseen or clearly seen, consistent with the two peaks observed in human observers visibility ratings (Dehaene et al., 2003). Global workspace theory has also helped advance research on machine consciousness. Blum and Blum (2022) formalised GWTs selection and broadcast mechanisms in the Conscious Turing Machine (CTM), an explicit computational model of consciousness. In this model, long-term memory (LTM) consists of many specialised processors, each with its own memory. processor submits information as chunk, short message containing its content and an assigned importance. Short-term memory (STM) serves as the shared workspace and holds one chunk at time. The Up Tree selects winning chunk through successive pairwise competitions, and chunks with higher competition scores are more likely to advance. The winning chunk enters STM, and the Down Tree broadcasts it to all LTM processors. The authors also used the basketball and gorilla example (Simons and Chabris, 1999) to illustrate this process. The instruction to count one teams passes is first broadcast to all processors. The visual processors then give greater 44 priority to information about that team. The gorilla chunk has little chance of entering STM and being broadcast, so the CTM fails to consciously notice the gorilla (Blum and Blum, 2022). The CTM gives GWT precise computational formulation, with explicit rules for competition, storage and broadcast. Beyond formal accounts of consciousness, GWT has also inspired neural network architectures that use shared workspaces to coordinate information processing. Goyal et al. (2022) added few shared memory slots to Transformers to coordinate information across input positions. Representations at different positions compete for write access, and each position reads the selected information to update its state. This design improved performance on visual reasoning tasks. VanRullen and Kanai (2021) proposed shared latent workspace to connect separately trained vision, language and other networks. The workspace would translate selected information from one network into representations usable by the other networks, implementing broadcast across modalities. To reduce dependence on paired image-text data, Devillers et al. (2025) trained mappings between frozen vision and language networks through shared workspace. They also trained the mappings to reconstruct each representation after translation to the other modality and back, which allowed learning from unpaired data and reduced the number of paired examples needed for alignment and translation. Fountas et al. (2026) built an explicit workspace, the Global Key-Value Workspace, into pretrained LLMs. Their method selects components from the key-value cache, writes them to the workspace and broadcasts the result back to all components. Their experiments showed improved reasoning performance, and selecting fewer components preserved much of the performance of full broadcast at lower computational cost. Another line of research examines the emergence of workspace-like organisation through LLM training. To study information integration, Urbina-Rodriguez et al. (2026) measured synergy between attention heads, which is information that the heads carry only in combination, not individually. They identified synergistic core in the middle layers of trained models, absent in randomly initialised models. The ablation of high-synergy heads disproportionately impaired mathematical reasoning. Reinforcement learning restricted to these heads also produced larger gains than training redundant or randomly selected heads. Gurnee et al. (2026) developed J-Lens to investigate global workspace structure and function in LLMs. They compared Jspace geometry across layers using CKA and examined concept readouts and representational capacity. These analyses identified an intermediate band of layers with coherent concept representations and limited capacity. Within this band, MLP layers amplified J-space directions far more strongly than random directions. subset of attention heads relayed J-space content across token positions. Both findings are consistent with GWTs broadcast mechanism. To study concept availability during reasoning, Chun et al. (2026) measured how easily the models internal states could be separated according to the value of an intermediate variable. The states were easy to separate while the model computed the variable and again when later step used it. In between, they were much harder to separate, although trained probes could still recover the variables value. The authors interpreted this pattern as the allocation of limited representational capacity to the current computation. In this paper, we extend this line of work to visual concepts in VLMs, examining selective access to these concepts under different questions and their availability to multiple downstream computations.

sections.title: 9.2 Mechanistic Interpretability
sections.content: A models final answer provides only limited view of its internal concept representations. To study these representations, researchers have developed methods for reading information from intermediate states. Alain and Bengio (2016) introduced linear classifier probes, training separate classifier on each layers activations while keeping the original network fixed. To discover features beyond predefined categories, Bricken et al. (2023) used sparse autoencoder 45 to decompose activations in one-layer language model. This revealed features for specific text patterns, and activating selected features steered generation towards the corresponding patterns. Another way to read an intermediate state is to express its content through the models own vocabulary. The Logit Lens (nostalgebraist, 2020) applies the models output mapping directly to each layers hidden states to track token predictions across layers. The Tuned Lens (Belrose et al., 2023) first applies learned transformation specific to each layer. Its readouts more closely match the models final token probabilities. Patchscopes (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024) inserts hidden state into decoding prompt and lets the model generate description of its content. Vocabulary readouts can also be constructed from the models Jacobians, which describe how changes in intermediate states affect its output. Hernandez et al. (2024) proposed the Attribute Lens to read attributes from entity representations. They constructed mapping by averaging Jacobians over examples of the same relation, such as musician-instrument pairs, allowing trumpet to be recovered from the representation of Miles Davis. Gurnee et al. (2026) applied the same averaging principle across prompts and token positions to construct J-Lens for reading concepts across contexts. J-Lens maps intermediate states into the final layers representation space and applies the models output mapping, revealing intermediate concepts omitted from answers in multi-hop reasoning. To further reduce noise in the averaged Jacobian, Yan et al. (2026) retained only the pairs of token positions with the largest Jacobian norms. Keeping the top 20% improved intermediate-concept recall on five of six tasks in Qwen3-8B. To improve readouts in early layers, Blank et al. (2026) introduced R-Lens, replacing ordinary gradients with coefficients computed using layer-wise relevance propagation. This reduced irrelevant tokens in the readouts and revealed some intermediate concepts earlier than J-Lens. The original J-Lens ranks individual vocabulary tokens (Gurnee et al., 2026). However, concepts name may span several tokens, and its representation may contain information beyond single name token. To recover complete concept names, Gong et al. (2026) introduced Concept Lens, using token readouts and the input context to propose candidates. It obtains each candidates representation from fixed prompt and scores it against the original hidden state. These representations support both multi-token concept readout and concept swaps. In VLMs, visual concept can also be expressed through different names and related semantic content. Our proposed MC-Lens therefore constructs set of vocabulary directions for each concept. Word-form selection collects alternative forms of its name, while greedy selection chooses directions that capture its representation, including directions for related concepts. We use these sets to read visual concepts and test their roles in downstream computation through counterfactual interventions. Reading concept from an intermediate state does not establish that the model uses it in downstream computation. Yang et al. (2024) used gradients to estimate whether stronger recall of an intermediate entity would support the second step of two-hop reasoning. Across the tested relations, they found substantial evidence for entity recall and moderate evidence for its subsequent use. Gurnee et al. (2026) tested intermediate concepts by swapping their JLens coordinates with those of alternative concepts. These swaps redirected two-hop answers and, in separate experiments, changed answers about different attributes of the same entity. Zahedi et al. (2026) compared concept swaps at different token positions in two-hop capital questions. The intermediate entity, state or country, was readable at both the city-name and final prompt positions, but swapping it at the city name redirected answers more often. To study the use of external evidence, Kawada and Kellis (2026) split the hidden state into the component reconstructed with J-Lens and the remaining component. They swapped each component between runs that accepted supplied answer and runs that did not. In Llama and Qwen, swapping the reconstructed components preserved the rate of accepting supplied answer, while swapping the remaining components reduced it. In this paper, we use counterfactual interventions to examine the role of visual concepts in VLM reasoning. We compare name46 token directions with broader concept direction sets and test the necessity and sufficiency of the selected information for correct answers. We also examine whether the same concept directions influence multiple downstream tasks and successive reasoning steps. Mechanistic interpretability studies have also examined how VLMs represent visual information and use it to answer questions. Fu et al. (2025) compared VLM answers with direct readouts from visual encoder features on the same tasks. These readouts achieved better task performance, and the relevant visual information remained accessible in the connector and decoder. To trace how visual information reaches the answer, Salazar et al. (2026) used activation patching between paired examples. They found that open-ended object recognition relied on image tokens, while spatial judgements used visual information transferred to question tokens. Krojer et al. (2026) introduced LatentLens to interpret visual tokens by comparing them with contextualised text It retrieved descriptions of image regions even in early layers, where direct representations. vocabulary projection was less informative. The authors also found that, during connector training, visual representations became interpretable first near the language models input and later in deeper layers. In this paper, we use our proposed MC-Lens to examine the development of cross-modal concept alignment and selective access during controlled vision-language alignment training. Our readouts show that concept accessibility improves early in training, while reliable selective access according to the question develops later.

sections.title: 10 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we introduce MC-Lens to access concept information from intermediate visual and language states in shared semantic space. Using MC-Lens, we examine concept accessibility and selective access, the role of concepts in downstream reasoning, the development of crossmodal alignment during training, and shared workspace functions across VLMs. Our work provides an experimental basis for studying GWT in multimodal artificial systems. It also opens way to investigate how GWT can guide improvements in cross-modal alignment. Further investigation of the mechanisms that make selected information available to different downstream processes could deepen our understanding of workspace functions and contribute to research on machine consciousness.

sections.content: A.1 Lens Fitting We fit the lenses using multimodal examples from A-OKVQA (Schwenk et al., 2022). Following the J-Lens reference implementation (Gurnee et al., 2026), we exclude padding, the first 16 sequence positions and the final sequence position from the decoder position sets defined in Section 2.1. These exclusions apply to the intermediate decoder positions for L-Lens and the final-layer decoder positions for both lenses. We number Transformer blocks from zero and extract states after each block. We also fit lenses to intermediate states within the connector, including states before and after its linear transformations and activation functions. We follow Equation 5 with = C. A.2 Greedy Selection for Interventions We use greedy selection to construct concept direction sets for both state reconstruction (Section 3.2) and counterfactual interventions (Section 5). In the procedure described in Section 2.3, each iteration selects vocabulary direction, refits the coefficients of all selected directions by NNLS, and updates the remaining difference. sections.title: B Supplementary Comparisons
sections.content: B.1 Stability of J-Space Geometry across Fitting-Set Sizes We examine whether the layerwise J-space organisation observed in Section 6.1 changes with the amount of data used to fit L-Lens. We fit L-Lens for Qwen3-VL-8B using 1, 5, 10, 100 and 1,000 prompts and compare vocabulary-direction geometry across decoder layers using CKA. Figure S1: Decoder J-space geometry across fitting-set sizes. Each panel compares vocabulary-direction geometry across decoder layers of Qwen3-VL-8B using CKA, with L-Lens fitted on prompts. Figure S1 shows that the broad distinction between early and late decoder layers is visible even with single fitting prompt. As the fitting set grows, the region of high similarity among early layers becomes clearer. With 100 prompts, the pattern already closely resembles that obtained with the 1,000 prompts used in the main analysis. The broad layerwise organisation is therefore preserved across the tested fitting-set sizes. B.2 Effects of Aggregation and Reference Centring on Visual Readout We examine how aggregation across image-token positions and reference centring affect wholeimage object readout. Using the images from Section 3.3, we compare reading the mean imagetoken state with reading each position separately and retaining each vocabulary tokens highest score across positions. We evaluate both approaches with and without reference centring. Without reference centring, both approaches yield low Pass @10 (Table S1). Centring substantially improves object-name readout from the mean state, but reduces Pass @10 when each vocabulary tokens highest score is taken across positions. These results support using the centred mean state for whole-image object readout, as in Section 3.3.
